Microsoft is clamping down on boot systems because they see it as a threat. In past versions of Windows, you could select boot options, and in later versions (like Windows 8+) manufacturers were able to put manual overrides into the UEFI Secure Boot section of the BIOS to allow the installation of other OSs. In newer versions they are clamping down on this and pushing manufacturers to lock the secure boot system, most likely through incentives, ensuring only Microsoft digitally signed systems boot properly. The direct line is that it prevents things like rootkits, which, in some situations is true. But, last I checked that really isn't very valid with most current boot systems, especially Linux. Some of the same issues that make a BIOS (and any available memory still available in that way, vulnerable) is still something exploitable with a Windows boot. Hey! Former Windows dev (lifetime Linux nut) here.

First off UEFI + secure boot are huge security enhancements. Enabling secure boot almost totally guarantees your computer is booting the image you told it to boot, not some compromised code a malicious individual placed on it without your knowledge.

The downside is companies like Microsoft use this to try and lock down machines to thier ecosystem.

Some Linux distros even offer signed keys so once you image your machine, you can guarantee that image is what's booting (you need to add the key to your UEFI).

Anyways here are some things you should check:

  • is your USB drive being formatted properly? Make sure it's bootable + a format that UEFI can read (fat or some derivative)
  • to be sure make it with a tool like DD, unetbootin or Rufus.
  • does your Linux distro support UEFI? Not all do. Some have specific images for UEFI, because they target old machines. Others will boot legacy then install UEFI in thier installers or only if you ask for it.
  • try disabling fast boot. It does some things that mess with Linux install disks.

If all else fails you will have a legacy boot setting in your startup options that will enable old school bios booting. Then your machine will boot anything. (It will might be called legacy boot, but some vendors call it different things.)
